sets.fov: Andromeda with frames. Deep-navy bg; a big tilted spiral galaxy (cream-white core, blue-white arms, brown dust lanes); setp.hub 0..1 = a tiny white square outline (Hubble's window) draws on near the core; setp.rom 0..1 = a big cyan rectangle (Roman's window, 2:1) draws on and glows around the core; setp.t 0..1 = slow camera push; setp.label 0|1 = small labels HUBBLE / ROMAN appear on the frames.
sets.grid: Tiling grid. Deep-navy bg; one big cyan-outlined 2:1 rectangle filled with a 10x10 grid of small white squares (a hundred); setp.fill 0..100 = squares light up gold one by one until that count; setp.zoom 0..1 = camera zooms from one square to the whole rectangle; setp.glow 'gold'|'cyan'.
sets.moonsky: Night sky size compare. Deep-navy starry sky over a dark horizon; a pale full Moon disc (about 0.5 degree) with a thin outline; setp.rom 0..1 = a long cyan rectangle drawn beside the Moon, slightly wider than the Moon, 2:1; setp.hub 0..1 = a tiny white square drawn on the Moon's face; setp.t 0..1 = slow pan.
sets.mirror: Telescope mirror close up. Deep-navy bg; a big round silver mirror, 4 px outline, hexagonal honeycomb ribs visible in a cutaway on one side, pale rim light and a slow glint sweep; setp.t 0..1 = glint sweeps across; setp.weight 0..1 = a small scale tips from a heavy dark block (Hubble 828 kg) toward a light one (Roman 186 kg); setp.bump 0|1 = a tiny bump on the surface is highlighted by a cyan callout.
sets.optics: Light path diagram. Deep-navy bg; a side view of a telescope tube with three curved mirrors (primary, secondary, tertiary) drawn as thick outlined curves and a gold ray bouncing through them to a small detector box; setp.t 0..1 = the gold ray travels; setp.wide 0..1 = the ray fans out into a wide cone; setp.short 0|1 = a cream bracket shows the focal length shrinking to a third.
sets.skyspeck: Whole-sky map. Deep-navy bg; a big dark oval all-sky map with faint stars and a thin cream grid; setp.cover 0..1 = a tiny gold patch (0.1 percent, Hubble's total) draws on; setp.rom 0..1 = a growing cyan area fills the map (50 times that patch); setp.t 0..1 = slow camera pull out.
sets.mosaic: Photo mosaic being stitched. Deep-navy bg; many small overlapping square photo tiles of a galaxy slowly pasting together into a big oval galaxy image; setp.tiles 0..600 = how many tiles are placed; setp.calendar 0..10 = a small year counter bar fills; setp.glow 0|1 = the finished galaxy glows.
sets.l2: Earth to L2 diagram. Deep-navy bg; on the left a small blue Earth with a tiny Moon on a thin ring, on the right a dotted halo-orbit ellipse around a small cyan marker labelled L2, a straight dashed line between; setp.t 0..1 = a tiny telescope icon (gold mirror) travels along the dashed line from Earth to L2; setp.halo 0..1 = it loops on the halo ellipse; setp.sun 0|1 = a warm light from the far left.
sets.pixelwall: A wall of pixels. Deep-navy bg; a huge mosaic grid of coloured square pixels of a deep-space image (galaxies as bright smudges); setp.zoom 0..1 = camera zooms into the grid until single pixels are big squares; setp.pick 0..1 = a white selection box drops onto one pixel and it glows gold; setp.card 0|1 = a small trading card flips up beside it.
sets.stream: A big screen live stream. Dark auditorium; far: a giant screen showing a starry placeholder with a cyan LIVE dot; mid: rows of silhouette chairs; near: floor plane with pale rim; setp.t 0..1 = the screen brightens; setp.count 0..1 = the countdown on the screen shrinks; setp.cheer 0|1 = silhouettes raise arms.
sets.zoomwide: Lens comparison. Deep-navy bg; two outlined camera lenses side by side: a short wide-angle lens on the left (cyan glow) and a long zoom lens on the right (white glow); setp.t 0..1 = left lens emits a wide cyan cone, right lens a thin white beam; setp.pick 'wide'|'zoom' = that lens glows brighter; setp.link 0|1 = a gold arrow links the two.
sets.lab: A bright astronomers' control room. far: wall of dark screens with soft cream charts and a world map; mid: a desk with two laptops, a coffee mug and a sticky note; near: carpet GroundPlane with pale rim; setp.alert 0..1 = a screen flashes amber with a warning triangle; setp.ok 1 = screens turn green.
sets.scope: A space telescope in deep space. far: SpaceBackdrop; mid: a Webb-style telescope with a hexagon-segment gold mirror, a flat layered silver sunshield and a small body, 4 px outline, pale rim light; setp.t 0..1 = slow drift; setp.look 0..1 = a faint cyan cone widens from the mirror toward the sky; setp.blink 0|1 = a camera flash.
sets.darkweb: Cosmic web. Deep-navy bg; a glowing network of cyan filaments with bright galaxy dots at the nodes and dark voids between; setp.t 0..1 = filaments slowly draw on; setp.warp 0..1 = the web bends and drifts outward; setp.glow 'gold'|'cyan'|'violet'.
sets.planet: A distant star with a planet. Deep-navy bg; a blinding white star on the left with spiky glare; a small blue-green planet on the right; setp.mask 0..1 = a black circular mask (coronagraph) grows over the star and the glare fades revealing the planet; setp.t 0..1 = slow drift.
sets.void: Plain deep-navy SpaceBackdrop stage with slow light rays and almost no stars, for big numbers, bars and diagrams. setp.glow 'gold'|'cyan'|'red' tints the rays.

props.starbig: Icon of a giant star: a big red-orange disc with soft glow, darker blotches and a 4 px outline; pp.s scale; pp.label text beneath.
props.starsmall: Icon of a small star: a bright yellow round disc with a soft glow and 4 px outline; pp.s scale; pp.label text beneath.
props.counter: Big flat panel, 4 px dark outline, dark #1E1B2E face, cream flip digits in FONTS.title with thousands separators, label in FONTS.ui underneath. pp.from and pp.to: the number counts from->to across the shot (ease-out); pp.label text; pp.color gold|red|cyan.
props.clock: Round analogue clock face, cream disc, 4 px dark outline, ticks, one hand. pp.from..pp.to in hours: the hand sweeps; pp.glow true adds a gold bloom.
props.bar: Horizontal progress bar with 4 px outline, filled with pp.color (gold|red|cyan) to pp.frac of its width over the shot; pp.label above in FONTS.ui.
props.arrow: Thick outlined curved arrow, pp.color gold|cyan|red, draws on across the shot.
props.flag: Small green check mark badge in a round outlined cream disc with a tiny sparkle; or red cross when pp.bad true.
props.calendar: Small wall calendar page, cream with a red top strip, 4 px outline; pp.text the date in FONTS.title (max 8 chars).
props.magnifier: Outlined magnifying glass with a cream handle and pale glass; pp.s scale; pp.glow true adds a cyan bloom in the lens.
props.spoon: A silver spoon with a dark 4 px outline, tilted; pp.s scale.
props.ring: Pulsing cyan circle outline, 4 px, soft bloom, that expands and fades each second; pp.s scale.
props.scale: Small balance scale icon, cream, 4 px outline, one pan tipped low; pp.s scale; pp.label text beneath.
props.camera: Overlay prop: a chunky outlined black digital camera with a big round lens and a gold shutter button, held in front of Pip's chest with both hands; pp.s scale.
props.shades: Overlay prop: dark rounded sunglasses sitting on Pip's face over the eyes, 4 px outline, with a tiny white glint; Pip's head and hood stay visible.

actions.lookup: Pip tilts head back (headTilt up), arms hang loose, small sway; eyes lift at p 0.2.
actions.duck: Pip drops into a crouch with both arms raised over the head at p 0.15 and holds with a small tremble.
actions.spin: Pip turns one slow full rotation (yaw/spin) across the shot while looking up.
actions.flinch: A quick squash and lean away at p 0.2 with arms up, then settles back by p 0.7.
actions.pointup: Pip's arm swings up to point at the sky at p 0.2 with a small overshoot.

chapters.title: ANDROMEDA
chapters.sub: Ten years or a few shots

film.vo: This tiny square is all Hubble sees in one shot. This is Roman's.
One hundred times the sky. Same mirror. Same sharpness.
NASA says the first pictures arrive on seventh December.
So what if you held that camera?
Welcome to Ifmosphere. Here are the rules.
You get two windows onto the sky, side by side.
Hubble's window is a sharp little square.
Roman's window is a giant, and it's real.
The rule is simple. Pick one, and the other waits.
Here is the catch. You have to understand why the big one works.
Start with Hubble. Its patch is zero point zero five six degrees wide.
film.dir: measured; stress 'zero point zero five six'

film.vo: That is a tenth the width of the full Moon.
One shot, sixteen megapixels. Your phone does more.
Now aim it at something huge, like the Andromeda galaxy.
In our sky it spreads three degrees. Six full Moons wide.
Hubble covers it a square at a time.
So Hubble's real answer was to just keep going.
Years of it. More than six hundred overlapping snapshots.
Over ten years, for one galaxy.
film.dir: flat, sets up the contrast; stress 'ten years'

film.vo: The result is gorgeous. Two point five billion pixels, two hundred million stars.
But you just spent a decade. Hold that thought.
Hubble is a zoom champion. In visible and ultraviolet light, nothing sharper exists.
Roman sees a tenth of an arcsecond per pixel. Hubble-sharp, in infrared.
Hubble sees ultraviolet, visible and near-infrared. Roman leans infrared.
Now switch windows. Roman's camera is the wide one.
Here is the twist. Roman's mirror is the same size as Hubble's.
Two point four metres across. Almost eight feet.
So where does a hundred times the sky come from?
Not from a bigger mirror. From a shorter focal length.
Hubble folds light off two mirrors. Roman uses three.
Roman's three mirrors shorten the focal length to a third.
Shorter focal length, wider view. It's a wide-angle lens in space.
Hubble is the zoom lens. Roman is the wide one.
And the mirror itself is the real flex. It weighs four times less.
One eighty-six kilograms against eight twenty-eight. Pip approves.
It is also absurdly smooth. Scale Earth up to that mirror's size.
The biggest bump on it would be a quarter of an inch.
Hubble's biggest bump, six inches. A speed hump for an ant.
So now you hold the wide window. What do you point it at?
Its mirror wears a silver coat, four hundred nanometres thick.
That is three hundred times thinner than a human hair.
Do the tiling. A hundred Hubble frames, ten by ten, fill Roman's.
The same galaxy that cost Hubble ten years.
Roman's window covers a huge slab of it at once.
Click. That's one picture.
Nudge the camera, click again. A few pointings and the whole galaxy's done.
Where Hubble needed ten years.
NASA says Roman surveys Andromeda nearly fifteen hundred times faster.
A decade becomes about two and a half days.
film.dir: awed; stress 'two and a half days'

film.vo: Quick honesty check. That last number is our maths, not NASA's.
film.dir: honest, quick aside; stress 'my own maths'

film.vo: Ten years divided by fifteen hundred is roughly two and a half days.
Whole sky now. Thirty years of Hubble: one tenth of one percent.
film.dir: sober; stress 'one tenth of one percent'

film.vo: In five years, Roman images fifty times what Hubble managed in thirty.
That's the trade. You give up zoom, and you get everything.
But a camera this good has to get to its spot first.
Two point five billion pixels, still only a fraction of Andromeda's stars.
Imagine what a wider window finds in all that light.
Hubble hugs Earth, about four hundred eighty kilometres up.
Roman flies a million miles out, to a spot called L two.
It launched on the thirtieth of August, on a Falcon Heavy.
Then a three-month trip, alone, through the dark.
At L two, the pull of the Sun and Earth balance.
It sits cold and steady, far from Earth's glow. Perfect for infrared.
Next door is Webb. Roman joins it out there.
Out there, the telescope switches on piece by piece.
Cameras, detectors, mirrors. Every one tested and tuned.
Eighteen detectors have to work as one camera.
Together they make two hundred eighty-eight megapixels.
Sixteen for Hubble. Two eighty-eight for Roman.
And in each frame, Roman's view is point eight by point four degrees.
A shade wider than the full Moon.
So the camera works. But what will it show first?
Parking there costs almost no fuel. The orbit practically holds itself.
No Earth glow, no Moon glare, just cold, quiet dark.
NASA is saving that for Monday, seventh December.
Three thirty in the afternoon, Eastern time.
That's eight thirty in the evening in London.
A live stream from a science conference in San Francisco.
And nobody outside the team has seen the pictures.
NASA hasn't even said where Roman looked. That's a real unknown.
So here's the fun part you can actually do. Claim a pixel.
Every pixel of those first images is a unique piece of the cosmos.

text.text: EACH PIXEL = A PIECE OF SKY

film.vo: Pick yours and it glows. You get a digital trading card.
Then you wait, with everyone else, for the stream.
You don't need a ticket. NASA streams it live on its own platforms.
People are even hosting watch parties for the reveal.
Roman isn't only here for pretty pictures.
In the nineteen nineties, astronomers found the universe's expansion is speeding up.
We call whatever drives that dark energy.
Roman's wide view will test whether dark energy changes over time.
It will also chart dark matter, which we only feel as gravity.
By watching how visible stuff moves, Roman reads the invisible stuff.
Roman also carries a coronagraph. Basically, a sun visor for planets.
It blocks the star's glare so a faint planet can show.
NASA says it's a hundred to a thousand times better than earlier ones.
Remember the catch? Roman can't zoom in like Hubble.
So Roman finds the interesting spots. And Hubble and Webb zoom in.
Wide to find it. Zoom to understand it.
Roman's camera can also split light into colours, across its whole view.
That reads motion, chemistry and temperature, everywhere at once.
And it keeps coming back, so the sky becomes a movie.
Hubble's archive shows change on a human timescale. Roman will stretch that far.
One more thing about the name.
Nancy Grace Roman was NASA's first chief astronomer.
People call her the mother of Hubble.
So Roman isn't a replacement. It's a wide-eyed sibling.
Roman will also catch subtle changes in our own Milky Way.
So back to that first square. Hubble's window.
That giant frame is the same mirror, bent a smarter way.
One hundred times the sky. Fifty times the coverage, in five years.
And on seventh December, we all finally get to look through it.
Which part of the sky do you want Roman to look at first?
Tomorrow: what if the Sun blinked out for one minute?

short.vo: You hold a camera that sees one hundred Hubbles at once.
Hubble sees this tiny square. Roman sees all of this.
Same two point four metre mirror.
The trick is three mirrors, and a focal length a third as long.
It sees in infrared, like Webb's cousin.
Hubble spent ten years stitching Andromeda.
Roman does it in a few clicks.
NASA says nearly fifteen hundred times faster.
Hubble has seen one tenth of one percent of the sky.
Roman will image fifty times that in five years.
Its first pictures drop on seventh December.
You can even claim one pixel.
It's named for NASA's first chief astronomer.
Tomorrow: what if the Sun blinked out for one minute?
One hundred Hubbles in one shot. Full film on the channel.
